Scales
SKALES
n. pl.
From Old French escale, a husk or shell. Webster 1828: the small shells or crusts which cover the skin of fishes and reptiles; also a thin lamina or flake. Distinct from scales the balance, which is from a different root.

Biblical Definition

Scales in Scripture are the plates that cover a fish or a monster, and the word appears in the food law, in the description of leviathan, and at the conversion of Paul. The dietary law makes them a test: whatsoever hath fins and scales in the waters, in the seas, and in the rivers, them shall ye eat (Leviticus 11:9), repeated at Deuteronomy 14:9. Fins and scales together mark a creature that keeps to its own element and moves through it in the ordered way; without both it was unclean to Israel. Job’s description of leviathan makes the scales an image of impenetrable pride: His scales are his pride, shut up together as with a close seal (Job 41:15) — a creature so armoured that no weapon reaches it, produced by God as the last argument in the whirlwind. And Luke uses the word for the moment Saul of Tarsus received his sight: immediately there fell from his eyes as it had been scales: and he received sight forthwith, and arose, and was baptized (Acts 9:18). The man who had been struck blind by the light of Christ’s glory sees again when Ananias, a disciple of the sect he had come to destroy, lays hands on him.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SCALE as the small shell or crust which composes a part of the covering of a fish or reptile; also, a thin lamina or flake. Webster distinguishes this word from scale, a balance, and scale, a ladder or graduated series.

expand to see more

SCALE, n. — The small shell or crust which forms part of the covering of a fish or a reptile.

A thin plate or lamina; a flake; anything resembling a fish’s scale in thinness and overlap.

Webster keeps this word distinct from SCALE, a balance for weighing, and from SCALE, a ladder or a graduated line.

In the Levitical law, fins and scales together were the mark of a clean water creature.

From Old French escale, a husk or shell — the root also of shell and scallop.

Key Scripture

Leviticus 11:9 — "These shall ye eat of all that are in the waters: whatsoever hath fins and scales in the waters, in the seas, and in the rivers, them shall ye eat."

Deuteronomy 14:9 — "These ye shall eat of all that are in the waters: all that have fins and scales shall ye eat:"

Job 41:15 — "His scales are his pride, shut up together as with a close seal."

Acts 9:18 — "And immediately there fell from his eyes as it had been scales: and he received sight forthwith, and arose, and was baptized."

Modern Corruption

The food laws are frequently offered as evidence that Scripture’s commands are arbitrary or merely hygienic, and both readings miss the stated purpose, which is to teach a people to distinguish.

expand to see more

Leviticus 11 gives its own reason at the end of the chapter: to make a difference between the unclean and the clean, because I am the LORD your God: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy. The laws trained a nation in discrimination — in the daily habit of asking what belongs to God’s people and what does not — and they marked Israel out visibly from every neighbour, since a nation that cannot eat with its neighbours will not intermarry with them either. The hygienic explanation is not the point and does not fit all the cases. And the arbitrariness objection misses that the ceremonial law was never permanent: Christ declared all meats clean (Mark 7:19), Peter was taught it on a rooftop, and the dictionary holds with the confession that the ceremonial laws are now abrogated while the moral law abides.

Acts 9:18 has been so worn by devotional use that its actual shape is worth restating. The scales did not fall from the eyes of a man who was groping toward the truth; they fell from a man who had been blinded for three days after meeting the risen Christ on a road he was travelling with warrants to arrest Christians. He did not reason his way in. He was struck down, named, blinded, and led by the hand into the city, and his sight was restored by a frightened disciple who had argued with God about going. That is what the Reformed tradition means by effectual calling, and Paul spent the rest of his life describing himself as one born out of due time and the least of the apostles because of it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qasqeseth (H7193), a scale of a fish; magen (H4043), a shield — used of leviathan’s scales; Greek lepis (G3013), a scale, a flake; pterugion, a fin.

expand to see more

Hebrew qasqeseth (H7193) — a fish scale; the term of Leviticus 11:9 and Deuteronomy 14:9.

Hebrew magen (H4043) — a shield; leviathan’s scales are literally his shields, shut up together as with a close seal (Job 41:15).

Greek lepis (G3013) — a scale, a flake; only at Acts 9:18.

Hebrew senappir (H5579) — a fin; the companion requirement to scales in the clean-creature test.

Hebrew badal (H914) — to divide, to separate; the verb of the law’s stated purpose, to make a difference.

Usage

"Whatsoever hath fins and scales… them shall ye eat (Leviticus 11:9) — a law that trained a nation to distinguish."

"His scales are his pride, shut up together as with a close seal (Job 41:15) — armour no weapon reaches."

"There fell from his eyes as it had been scales (Acts 9:18) — sight restored to a man struck blind on his way to arrest Christians."
